sections.h2: What the planner does, step by step
p: Step one adds up the appliances you tick: the watts that run at once and the units they use in a day. Step two sizes the inverter for that running load with a safety margin, and step four can raise it so the inverter accepts the solar array. Step three sizes the battery for only the load you want to keep on during loadshedding, for the hours you choose. Step four sizes the solar array for your daily units and your city's sun. Step five splits a month's solar between what you use while the sun is up and what you export, and compares the energy charge with and without net billing. Step six sizes a generator for the whole list, in case you want one for long outages.
Every step is a calculator on this site. Open any of them from the task cards below to change its assumptions, see worked examples and read the formula.

Start with the task, not the jargon. If the lights go out during loadshedding, start with the battery and UPS tools. If the bill is the problem, start with the bill calculators and the AC consumption tool. If you are planning solar, add up your home load first, then size the system.

Each result page ends with a Next step link to the tool that naturally follows, so a battery backup time leads to inverter sizing, a home load leads to solar sizing, and a wire size leads to the breaker to pair with it.

sections.h2: Why the numbers can be trusted
p: The calculators share one engine with one set of formulas and one set of constants. The same formula produces the live result, the worked examples, the reference tables and the FAQ answers on every page, so no two pages can disagree.

The formulas follow standard electrical practice (IEC and NEPRA performance standards for a 230 V, 400 V three-phase, fifty hertz supply). Assumptions that depend on judgement are marked and editable, and a review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress.

faq.q: Can I save or share my plan?
faq.a: Yes. Press the plan button, then use Save as PDF to print or keep the page, WhatsApp to send the sizes and a link to your installer, or copy the link: it carries your appliance list, so whoever opens it sees the same plan.

faq.q: Why is the saving an energy-charge estimate only?
faq.a: The planner compares only the energy charge of 396 units with the net-billing energy charge after 198 self-used and 223 exported units. Fixed charge, per-unit surcharges and GST are left out; most of them also fall when you import fewer units, so the real saving is usually somewhat higher than this estimate. The buyback rate is editable because it is not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page.
Yes. Every tool runs in your browser, needs no sign-up and stores nothing about you. You can share a result by copying the page link after you press Calculate.

faq.q: Do the tools work outside Pakistan?
faq.a: Yes. The defaults are set for Pakistan (230 V single phase, rupees, local tariff slabs), and the converters, battery, solar and wiring tools let you switch to 120 V or enter your own voltage and prices.

They are planning estimates built on typical values. Real backup time, bills and solar output depend on battery age, weather, the exact appliance and the tariff of the month, so expect the real number to land near the estimate, not exactly on it.

faq.q: Who writes and checks the tools?
faq.a: Wattlyst is written by its founder, Ali Ahmad, with formulas documented on the methodology page. Technical review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress and will be named on each page once complete.

key_facts: The planner carries one appliance list through the whole chain: running load, inverter, battery, solar, net billing and generator, each with the formula of its own calculator, so the sizes never contradict each other.

Inverter size = running watts × 1.25, raised if needed so the solar array is at most 1.3 times it; battery Ah = backup watts × hours ÷ (bank volts × usable depth of discharge × inverter efficiency); solar kW = the larger of daily units ÷ city yield and running watts ÷ performance ratio, with net billing counting the array only up to the sanctioned load; generator kVA = the larger of running × 1.25 and the starting peak, ÷ 0.8.
Default values (inverter efficiency 85% UPS and 90% hybrid, usable battery capacity 50% tubular and 90% lithium, power factor 0.8) are listed on the methodology page and editable in each calculator.
Pakistan tariff slabs, peak sun hours by city and appliance wattages live in dated data files; the net-billing buyback rate is not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page and stays editable.
Results are planning estimates, not an official bill or an engineer's design; wiring and solar work must be confirmed by a licensed electrician.

Inverter: the larger of {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{in.margin|2}} = {{out.inverter_kw_load|2}} kW and the solar array ÷ {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} = {{out.inverter_kw_array|2}} kW (an inverter accepts panels up to about that many times its rating), so {{out.inverter_kw|up1}} kW. Battery: {{in.backup_w}} W × {{in.backup_hours|1}} h = {{out.backup_kwh|2}} kWh ÷ ({{out.battery_v}} V × {{out.battery_dod|pct}} usable × {{d.inverter_eff_hybrid|pct}} inverter) = {{out.battery_ah|up}} Ah. Solar: energy {{out.daily_kwh|1}} kWh ÷ {{out.city_yield|1}} kWh per kW per day = {{out.solar_kw_energy|2}} kW; midday power {{out.running_w|int}} W ÷ {{out.pr|2}} performance ratio = {{out.solar_kw_power|2}} kW; the larger, {{out.solar_kw|2}} kW, needs {{out.panels|int}} panels of {{out.panel_w|int}} W = {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW making about {{out.monthly_solar_kwh|int}} units a month. Net billing counts an array up to your {{out.sanctioned_kw|1}} kW sanctioned load: {{out.net_billing_panels|int}} panels, {{out.net_billing_kw|2}} kW, about {{out.net_billing_solar_kwh|int}} units a month. You use {{out.self_used_units|int}} of those units yourself, export {{out.export_units|int}} at {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} and import {{out.import_units|int}}; energy charge {{out.bill_before_rs|rs}} before solar, {{out.bill_after_rs|rs}} after, saving {{out.saving_rs|rs}} a month on the energy charge alone. Generator for the whole list: {{out.generator_kva|1}} kVA, next standard size {{out.generator_pick_kva|1}} kVA.
how.text: Your list runs 2,085 W at once (2,535 W when the biggest motor starts) and uses 13.2 units a day, 396 a month. Inverter: the larger of 2,085 W × 1.25 = 2.61 kW and the solar array ÷ 1.3 = 2.7 kW (an inverter accepts panels up to about that many times its rating), so 2.7 kW. Battery: 500 W × 4 h = 2 kWh ÷ (24 V × 90% usable × 90% inverter) = 103 Ah. Solar: energy 13.2 kWh ÷ 4 kWh per kW per day = 3.3 kW; midday power 2,085 W ÷ 0.78 performance ratio = 2.67 kW; the larger, 3.3 kW, needs 6 panels of 585 W = 3.51 kW making about 421 units a month. Net billing counts an array up to your 4 kW sanctioned load: 6 panels, 3.51 kW, about 421 units a month. You use 198 of those units yourself, export 223 at Rs 11.00 and import 198; energy charge Rs 14,449 before solar, Rs 3,275 after, saving Rs 11,174 a month on the energy charge alone. Generator for the whole list: 3.3 kVA, next standard size 3.5 kVA.

content.answer: The Home Power Planner sizes everything from one appliance list: a typical home running 2,085 W needs about a 2.7 kW inverter, a 103 Ah battery for 4 hours of backup, a 3.51 kW solar system of 6 panels that saves about Rs 11,174 a month in energy charge under net billing, and a 3.5 kVA generator. Edit the list and every size updates. Each number links to the full calculator with its formula.
